# CharacterCursor

[Toolkit](README.md) · `DotGame.Toolkit.Fonts` · record struct

```csharp
public readonly record struct CharacterCursor
```

Identifies the position of a character within the original text being drawn.

## Remarks

Both indexes are absolute: they are relative to the start of the original text, not to the start of the span passed to a draw method. This allows a single [`ICharacterAttributes`](ICharacterAttributes.md) instance to describe text that is drawn in several pieces (for example, one piece per wrapped line) without splitting the attributes.

[`CharIndex`](#charindex) identifies the position within the text as it was written, and [`GlyphIndex`](#glyphindex) identifies the position within the text as it is drawn. Use the former to describe a range of the text, and the latter to distribute an effect evenly across the text.

Additional position information should be added here rather than as extra parameters, so that the cursor can grow without breaking every implementation.

## Constructors

```csharp
public CharacterCursor(int charIndex, int glyphIndex)
```

Makes a cursor at these positions.

```csharp
public CharacterCursor(int charIndex, int glyphIndex, float x)
```

Makes a cursor at these positions, on a character at `x` along its line.

## Properties

### CharIndex

```csharp
public int CharIndex { get; }
```

Gets the UTF-16 index of the character within the original text.

This is the index that a caller uses to describe a range of the text, so it counts each character of a surrogate pair separately, exactly as `string` does.

### GlyphIndex

```csharp
public int GlyphIndex { get; }
```

Gets the ordinal of the glyph within the original text.

This counts Unicode code points, so a surrogate pair counts once while an emoji sequence counts each of its code points: [`SpriteFont`](SpriteFont.md) does no text shaping, so it forms no ligatures or sequences. That makes this the useful index for effects that distribute an attribute evenly across the text, such as a per-glyph color ramp.

The ordinal increases as the text is drawn. Whether characters that draw nothing, such as a line break or a character that is missing from the font, advance the ordinal is unspecified, so treat it as a position rather than as a count.

### Start

```csharp
public static CharacterCursor Start { get; }
```

The start of a text.

### X

```csharp
public float X { get; }
```

Gets how far along its line the middle of the character's advance is, from the start of the piece of text being drawn, in pixels of the font's native size.

What attributes that place characters by where they are need: text along a curve turns and moves each character by how far it is from the line's middle. It's also the point a character's [`ICharacterAttributes.Rotation`](ICharacterAttributes.md#rotation) turns it about, on the baseline.
